newsitem.title: BULGARIA: BULGARIA IN TALKS WITH RUSSIA TO BUY MIG-29SMS.
newsitem.headline: BULGARIA IN TALKS WITH RUSSIA TO BUY MIG-29SMS.

text.p: Bulgaria is in talks with Russia to buy 14 modern MiG-29SM jet fighters and set up a joint venture in the town of Plovdiv to overhaul MiG planes, deputy defence minister Simeon Petkovski said on Tuesday.

Petkovski said Moscow had offered Sofia a $450 million credit to buy the planes. Part of the credit could go towards developing an international service centre for MiGs at the existing Aviotechnica aviation plant in Plovdiv.

Bulgaria's interim cabinet last month made a clear statement of its desire to join NATO, an issue on which the previous Socialist government had been ambivalent for fear of upsetting their traditional allies in Moscow, which opposes NATO's eastward expansion.

"Talks have been on for a year and we think that this is a favourable deal, but it is only parliament which can approve the credit," Petkovski told Reuters. "We need the planes but we have agreed only in principle."
Bulgarian parliamentary elections are due on April 19.

The strategy planning director of the Moscow Aviation Production Union (MAPO), Alexander Ageev, told reporters in Sofia on Monday that buying Russian MiGs would not hinder Bulgaria's NATO membership application as the planes were considered to be among the best in the world.
"A country with developed aviation will have fewer financial difficulties in joining NATO, and during our talks we even raised the position that without MiGs you will not enter NATO," Ageev said.
The armed forces of ex-Warsaw Pact member Bulgaria are suffering the same economic crisis as the rest of the country.
Ageev said the plant could earn money for Bulgaria by servicing planes from other Balkan countries, the Near East, North Africa and Asia.
MAPO, which unites the MiG and Kamov design bureaux and several aviation plants, was willing to supply more equipment for the plant, and Ageev said the credit conditions would be favourable.

"The loan will be paid in more than 10 years after sealing the deal and the grace period will be until 2001...by when Bulgaria's economy will be standing on its own feet," Ageev told Standart daily newspaper.
He said the decision on the credit had been taken in 1996 and Russia was urging Bulgaria to make a decision so that the sum could be included in the Russian budget.
Petkovski said the plan was to establish a joint venture or joint stock company at the Plovdiv plant.
